title: The <head> and Metadata
summary: The head contains information about a page that is not part of its visible content.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: `<title>` names the page in the browser tab, history, and bookmarks. A useful title tells people which page they opened. It is like writing a clear title on a folder. Give each important page a distinct title and avoid stuffing it with repeated keywords. For example, give the page a distinct title that matches the visible main heading.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: Character encoding tells the browser how to read bytes as text. UTF-8 supports the characters used by most languages. It is like agreeing on the alphabet before reading a note. Declare it early in the head so punctuation and international text display correctly. For example, declare the page language so speech tools can select suitable pronunciation.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: The viewport setting tells a mobile browser how to size the page layout. Without it, a phone may render a desktop-sized page and shrink it. It is like choosing the right paper size before laying out a document. Include the standard responsive viewport metadata and test at narrow widths. For example, set a viewport so a phone uses its actual device width.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: A description can summarize a page for search and sharing previews. Search engines may choose other text, so the description is not a guaranteed snippet. It is like a short back-cover summary. Make it accurate and specific to the page, and do not promise content the page does not provide. For example, write a description that accurately summarizes the current page content.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Keep metadata honest and current. A stale page title or inaccurate description creates confusion before someone even reads the content. This is like labeling a box with what is actually inside. Check titles, descriptions, language, and social preview data when a page is renamed or repurposed. For example, do not use metadata to claim content that visitors cannot find on the page.

foundations.overview: Metadata is information about a page that appears in browser tabs, search previews, and device layouts. Most metadata lives in the HTML `<head>`, away from the visible article content. Think of it as the label on a book: it helps people and tools identify the page. Keep titles accurate, declare text encoding, and set a viewport for mobile screens.
foundations.whyItMatters: Metadata helps browsers and discovery tools identify a page, but it must match accessible page content. Accurate metadata improves context without replacing useful content or security.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser parses <head> first, before rendering content. It uses charset to decode text, the viewport tag to set the layout viewport, <link rel=stylesheet> to fetch CSS, and <title> for the tab — so the head shapes how the body is interpreted and displayed.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every web page has a head: a title and description for SEO, the viewport tag for responsive design, favicon and stylesheet links, and often Open Graph/Twitter meta for social previews and analytics scripts.
foundations.businessImpact: Strong titles and descriptions raise search click-through and traffic; a correct viewport tag means the site actually works on the majority of users who are on mobile — both directly affect reach and revenue.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A consistent head template (charset, viewport, title, description, stylesheet links) is the baseline of every page or layout component, and frameworks centralize it so every route gets correct metadata.
foundations.performanceImpact: The head controls early loading: putting charset first avoids re-decoding, stylesheet links in head let CSS load early, and preconnect/preload hints in the head can speed up critical resources.
commonUseCases: Setting the page title for tabs, bookmarks, and search results
Declaring utf-8 encoding so text renders correctly
Adding the viewport meta tag for responsive mobile layout
Providing a meta description for the search snippet
Linking stylesheets, favicons, and analytics scripts

commonMisconceptions.myth: Content in the <head> shows up on the page.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The head is not rendered as page content. With the rare exception of how <title> appears in the tab, head elements describe or support the page — visible content goes in the <body>.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The meta description directly improves search ranking.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It doesn't directly affect ranking, but it's often shown as the result snippet, so a good description raises click-through rate.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The viewport tag is optional if your CSS is responsive.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render at a zoomed-out desktop width and your responsive breakpoints won't apply as intended.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A meta description guarantees the exact search result snippet.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Search engines may select other content and decide whether to show a rich result.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A noindex setting keeps private information safe.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Indexing directives do not restrict access; protect private routes with authorization.

visualExplorer.title: What goes in the <head> and why
visualExplorer.caption: The handful of metadata elements that make up a solid document head, in the order they typically appear.

config.intro: A well-formed <head> declares a few key pieces of metadata before any visible content is parsed.

steps.name: Charset first
steps.detail: <meta charset="utf-8"> comes first so the browser decodes all following text correctly.

steps.name: Viewport
steps.detail: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> sets up responsive layout on mobile.

steps.name: Title
steps.detail: <title> names the page for the tab, bookmarks, history, and search results.

steps.name: Description
steps.detail: <meta name="description"> gives search engines a snippet to show under the result.

steps.name: Links & scripts
steps.detail: <link rel="stylesheet"> for CSS, <link rel="icon"> for the favicon, and any <script> references.

interactiveExamples.title: A complete document head
interactiveExamples.explanation: This is the standard head every page should start with: charset, viewport, a descriptive title, and a description. Only the body content is visible — the head shapes how it's rendered and described.

files.index.html:
Welcome to Acme

The title above appears in the browser tab, not on the page.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The page shows the heading and paragraph; the browser tab reads 'Acme — Simple Invoicing'.

interactiveExamples.title: Why charset matters
interactiveExamples.explanation: With utf-8 declared, special characters render correctly. The charset must be in the head and ideally first, so the browser decodes the rest of the document properly.

files.index.html:
Accented text: café, naïve, résumé

Symbols: € £ ¥ — “smart quotes”

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Accented characters and currency symbols display correctly rather than as garbled mojibake.

codeLab.title: Build a proper head
codeLab.instructions: This page is missing key metadata. Add (in order) a utf-8 charset, the responsive viewport meta tag, a descriptive <title>, and a <meta name="description"> summarizing the page.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The tab shows a descriptive title; text renders correctly; the page is mobile-ready with a description for search.

files.index.html:
Bean & Brew Coffee

Fresh-roasted beans delivered weekly.

hints: Put <meta charset="utf-8"> first inside the head.
The viewport tag uses content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1".
Give the page a unique, descriptive <title> and a short <meta name="description">.

keyTakeaways: `<title>` names the page in the browser tab, history, and bookmarks.
Character encoding tells the browser how to read bytes as text.
The viewport setting tells a mobile browser how to size the page layout.
A description can summarize a page for search and sharing previews.
